Autoantibodies to GAD and Cell Surface
Determinants in Stiff Person Syndrome 7hashi
Chang, Philippa Pettingill, Haris Alexopoulos, Leslie W. Jacobson,
Oxford, United Kingdom, Peter Brown, London, United Kingdom,
Angela Vincent, Oxford, United Kingdom
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the role of autoantibodies (Abs) and GAD-
induced immunity in causing the stiff person syndrome (SPS). BACK-
GROUND: SPS is a highly disabling neurological disorder of the CNS
characterised by progressive muscular rigidity and spasms. The brainstem
is a likely site for pathology because of the presence of inhibitory centres
that exert suprasegmental inhibitory control on spinal circuits. Autoanti-
bodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD, the enzyme that synthesises
the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA) are detected in approximately 80%
of patients with SPS. However, because GAD is an intracellular protein, it
is not clear how it can be targeted by circulating autoantibodies. There
could be other autoantibodies or immune mechanisms in SPS that are
pathogenic and GADAbs could merely represent an epiphenomenon. DE-
SIGN/METHODS: Sera from 25 SPS patients were studied. GADAb titres
were titrated in radioimmunoprecipitation assays. Patient sera were re-
acted with murine primary neuronal cultures. Clinical phenotype, inflam-
matory markers and neuronal loss in CNS of mice passively transferred
with purified SPS patient IgG and mice actively immunised against GAD65
were compared with controls. RESULTS: GADAbs at high titre (median
7500 U/ml) showed 100% sensitivity in clinically well-defined classical SPS
and 76% sensitivity in the total SPS cohort. SPS sera contained antibodies
in addition to GADAbs that bound to cell surface epitopes of GABAergic
neurons. Passive transfer of SPS IgG did not induce disease in mice, but
